meters.label: Attack requests reaching the service per tick

frames.narration: Normal day: 200 legitimate requests per tick. 60 home users send 2 each from their own IPs, and an office of 40 people sends 80 through one NAT address. All are served.

A volumetric flood of about 5,000 units hits a 1,000 unit link. The link drops packets without caring who sent them, so only 19% of legitimate requests survive. A firewall behind the link cannot help: it only sees what got through.

Move the front door: announce the same address from 8 sites with anycast, each with 1,000 units of capacity, and scrub there. The flood is split and mostly dropped at the edge: with the toy's made-up scrubbing figures, 98% of legitimate requests are served and 2% are lost to false positives. Double the flood and the edge itself saturates: 78%.

A SYN flood is small in bandwidth but fills the 1,024 entry half-open table with spoofed entries that live 5 ticks. Legitimate SYNs find no free slot: 6% served. Every spoofed packet has a new source, so blocking IPs cannot match them.
SYN cookies keep no state until a valid ACK comes back, and spoofed senders never answer. All legitimate connections are served: 100%, with 0 attack entries held.

An HTTP flood: 500 real bot IPs each send 4 valid requests, 2,000 per tick against capacity 600. Legitimate requests are crowded out: 27% served. Blocking the 10 busiest IPs removes the office (80 requests) and 9 bots: 17% served. A per-IP limit of 3 gives 22%, since the bots stay under it.

A challenge that, in this toy, 95% of people pass and only 10% of bots do cuts the attack to 196 requests per tick and restores 95% of legitimate traffic. It still costs 5% of real users, which is the price of every filter: choose it knowing who pays.
